source_text: Eadem igitur forma, caetera quoque ad martyrii pertinere defendimus. Qui pluris, inquit, fecerit etiam animam suam quam me, non est me dignus; id est, qui maluerit vivere me negando, quam mori confitendo. Qui animam suam invenerit, perdet illam; qui vero perdiderit mei caussa, inveniet illam. Proinde enim invenit eam, qui negarit lucrifaciendo vitam; sed perdet in gehennam, qui se putat negando lucrifacere eam. Perdet autem eam ad praesens, qui confessus occiditur; sed inventurus eam in vitam aeternam. Ipsi denique praesides, cum hortantur negationi, serva animam tuam, dicunt, et noli animam tuam perdere. Quo modo loqueretur Christus, nisi quo modo tractaretur christianus? Sed cum prohibet meditari responsionem ad tribunal, famulos suos instruit, Spiritum Sanctum responsurum repromittit; et cum in carcere fratrem vult visitari, confessoris imperat curam; et cum Deum vindictam facturum electorum suorum affirmat, passiones consolatur illorum: etiam in parabola seminis post cespitem arefacti, persecutionum figurat ardorem. Haec si non ita accipiuntur quemadmodum pronuntiantur, sine dubio praeterquam sonant sapiunt; et aliud in vocibus erit, aliud in sensibus; ut allegoriae, ut parabolae, ut aenigmata. Quemcumque igitur conceperint ventum argumentationis scorpii isti, quocumque se acumine impegerint, una jam linea est: ad ipsas res provocabuntur, an secundum Scripturas transigantur. Siquidem tunc aliud significabitur in Scripturis, si non idipsum reperiatur in rebus. Quod enim scriptum est, hoc evenire oportebit. Porro, tunc eveniet quod est scriptum, si non aliud eveniet. Ecce autem et odio habemur ab omnibus hominibus, nominis caussa, quomodo et scriptum est; et tradimur etiam a proximis, quomodo et scriptum est; et perducimur ad potestates, et interrogamur, et torquemur, et confitemur, et trucidamur, quomodo et scriptum est. Sic Dominus edixit. Si aliter edixit haec, cur non aliter eveniunt, quam edixit, id est, quemadmodum edixit? Atquin non aliter eveniunt quam edixit: ergo sicut eveniunt, ita edixit, ita eveniunt. Nam nec licuisset aliter evenire, quam edixit; nec ipse aliter edixisset, quam evenire voluisset. Ita, non aliud significabunt Scripturae, quam in rebus recognoscimus. Aut si nondum aguntur illa quae praedicantur, quomodo haec aguntur quae praedicata non sunt? Non sunt enim haec praedicata quae aguntur, si alia sunt quae praedicantur, et non haec quae aguntur. At nunc, quia ipsa sunt in rebus, quae in vocibus, aliter dicta creduntur; quid fieret si aliter facta invenirentur? Sed haec est perversitas fidei, probata non credere, non probata praesumere. Cui perversitati illud quoque opponam, ut si haec quae sic aguntur quemadmodum scripta sunt, non erunt ipsa quae praedicantur, illa quae non debeant sic agi quemadmodum scripta sunt, ne et ipsa horum exemplo periclitentur, excludi siquidem aliud in vocibus, aliud in rebus est; et relinquitur nec praedicata videri cum evenerint, si aliter praedicantur quam evenire habent. Et quomodo credentur quae non erunt praedicata, quia non ita erunt praedicata quomodo eveniunt? Ita haeretici quae praedicantur non ut probata sunt credendo, ea quae nec praedicata sunt, credunt.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore we defend that the same form also pertains to the other things of martyrdom. He who does more, he says, and also makes his soul more than me, is not worthy of me, that is, he who prefers to live by denying me rather than to die by confessing. He who finds his soul will lose it; he who loses it for my sake will find it. Therefore he finds it who denies it by gaining life; but he loses it in Gehenna who thinks he gains it by denying. But he loses it now who is killed after confessing; but he will find it in eternal life. The judges themselves, when they encourage denial, say 'save your soul' and 'do not lose your soul'. How would Christ speak, if not in the way a Christian is treated? But when he forbids meditating on a response to the tribunal, he instructs his servants, promises that the Holy Spirit will respond; and when he wants a brother to be visited in prison, he commands care for the confessor; and when he affirms that God will avenge his elect, he consoles their passions: and also in the parable of the seed after the thorns are dried up, he figures the ardor of persecutions. If these things are not accepted as they are pronounced, without doubt they sound otherwise than they are wise; and one thing will be in the voices, another in the senses; like allegories, like parables, like enigmas. Whomever therefore these scorpions have conceived a wind of argument, with whatever sharpness they thrust themselves, now there is one line: they will be provoked to the things themselves, whether they are transacted according to the Scriptures. If indeed then something else will be signified in the Scriptures, if the same thing is not found in the things. For what is written, this ought to happen. Moreover, then it will happen what is written, if something else does not happen. Behold, we are also hated by all men, for the sake of the name, as it is written; and we are betrayed even by those near to us, as it is written; and we are led to the authorities, and questioned, and tortured, and confess, and are slaughtered, as it is written. So the Lord decreed. If he decreed these things otherwise, why do they not happen otherwise than he decreed, that is, as he decreed? But they do not happen otherwise than he decreed: therefore as they happen, so he decreed, so they happen. For it was not permitted to happen otherwise than he decreed; nor would he have decreed otherwise than he wanted to happen. So the Scriptures will not signify anything else than what we recognize in the things. Or if those things which are predicted are not yet done, how are these things done which are not predicted? For these things which are done are not predicted, if other things are predicted and not these things which are done. But now, because the same things are in the things as in the voices, otherwise spoken things are believed; what would happen if otherwise done things were found? But this is the perversity of faith, not to believe proven things, to presume unproven things. To which perversity I will also oppose this, that if these things which are done thus as they are written are not the same things which are predicted, those things which ought not to be done thus as they are written, lest they also be endangered by the example of these, if indeed another thing is excluded in the voices, another in the things; and it remains that predicted things are not seen when they happen, if they are predicted otherwise than they are going to happen. And how will those things be believed which are not predicted, because they are not predicted thus as they happen? So heretics believe those things which are predicted not as they have been proven by believing, but those things which are not predicted.

pass_b_english: We defend the same pattern in everything else that belongs to martyrdom. "Whoever does more," he says, "and makes his own soul count for more than me, is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:39). That is, whoever prefers to live by denying me rather than to die by confessing me. "Whoever finds his life will lose it; whoever loses it for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25; Luke 17:33). So the one who denies Christ to gain his life actually finds it — but only to lose it in Gehenna. The one who thinks he gains it by denying Christ loses it there. But the one who is killed after confessing loses his life now, yet will find it in eternal life.

Even the judges themselves, when they urge denial, say, 'Save your soul, and do not lose your soul.' How else would Christ speak than in the way a Christian is treated? When he forbids rehearsing a defense before the tribunal, he instructs his servants and promises the Holy Spirit will speak for them. When he wants a brother visited in prison, he commands care for the confessor. When he affirms that God will avenge his elect, he consoles their sufferings. Even in the parable of the seed after the thorns wither, he depicts the heat of persecutions (Matthew 13:6).

If these words are not taken exactly as they are spoken, they certainly sound different from what they mean; one thing will be in the words, another in the senses — like allegories, like parables, like riddles. Whatever scorpion has conceived a wind of argument for them, whatever sharpness they thrust themselves with, there is now a single line: they will be driven to the things themselves, to see whether they are carried out according to the Scriptures.

For if something else is signified in the Scriptures, but the same thing is not found in the events, then what is written will not happen. What is written must happen. And it will happen what is written — if nothing else happens instead. Look: we are hated by all people for the name's sake, just as it is written (Matthew 10:22). We are betrayed even by those closest to us, just as it is written (Matthew 24:9). We are hauled before authorities, interrogated, tortured, we confess, and we are slaughtered — just as it is written. So the Lord decreed.

If he decreed these things differently, why do they not happen differently than he decreed — that is, exactly as he decreed? But they do not happen differently than he decreed. Therefore, as they happen, so he decreed; so they happen. It was not permitted for them to happen otherwise than he decreed; nor would he have decreed otherwise than he wanted them to happen. Thus the Scriptures will not signify anything other than what we recognize in the events.

Or if the things predicted are not yet done, how are these things done which were not predicted? For the things that are happening are not predicted if other things are predicted and not these things that are happening. But now, because the same things are in the events as in the words, people believe things spoken otherwise. What would happen if the events themselves turned out differently? But this is the perversity of faith: not to believe proven things, to presume unproven things.

To that perversity I also oppose this: if these things that are happening exactly as written are not the very things predicted, then those things that ought not to happen exactly as written — lest they also be endangered by the example of these — must be excluded. For one thing is in the words, another in the events. And it remains that predicted things are not recognized when they happen, if they are predicted otherwise than they come to pass. And how will those things be believed which are not predicted, because they are not predicted in the way they happen? So heretics believe the things predicted not as they have been proven by believing, but the things that are not predicted at all.

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Latin text. Pass B provides necessary scripture citations (Matthew 10:39, Matthew 16:25, Luke 17:33, Matthew 13:6, Matthew 10:22, Matthew 24:9) which are required by the instructions to identify the content being quoted or alluded to. Pass A is a faithful literal gloss. The complex logical argument regarding 'things in the words' vs 'things in the events' (in rebus) is preserved in both.
